patterns.title: Binary Search on a Boundary
patterns.model: Maintain a known-false prefix and known-true suffix.
patterns.template: lo=0; hi=n; while lo<hi: mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2; if P(mid): hi=mid; else: lo=mid+1
patterns.example: Find the first timestamp at or after a request.

patterns.title: Shortest-Path Relaxation
patterns.model: Tentative distances are costs of discovered paths; settle the smallest.
patterns.template: pop minimum; skip stale; for each edge: improve and push
patterns.example: Find cheapest transit through a weighted directed network.
mistakes: Using a FIFO queue for arbitrary weights
Marking a node final on discovery

patterns.title: 0/1 Choice DP
patterns.model: Separate decisions by item prefix so each item can contribute once.
patterns.template: for each item: for capacity descending: dp[c]=max(dp[c],value+dp[c-weight])
patterns.example: Select jobs under a fixed memory budget.
mistakes: Treating capacity magnitude as input bit length

patterns.title: Restore a Structural Invariant
patterns.model: First perform a local update, then repair metadata and balance on the ancestor path.
patterns.template: update child; recompute height; inspect balance; rotate; return new subtree root
patterns.example: Maintain a dynamic ordered set with predictable lookup latency.
mistakes: Updating parent height before child height

patterns.title: Scan an Excluded Prefix
clues: Need the first valid original position
patterns.model: The current index separates candidates already ruled out from candidates still possible.
patterns.example: Find the earliest matching event in an unsorted log without changing its positions.
mistakes: Returning absence after only one mismatch

patterns.title: Reverse a Linked Chain
clues: Existing node identities must be preserved
Only constant auxiliary storage is allowed
patterns.model: A reversed prefix and unprocessed suffix partition the original nodes; preserve the next suffix root before rewiring.
patterns.template:
prev ← null; curr ← head
while curr ≠ null:
    successor ← curr.next
    curr.next ← prev
    prev ← curr
    curr ← successor
return prev
patterns.example: Reverse a singly linked chain without copying payloads or allocating replacements.
mistakes: Overwrite the successor before saving it

comparisons.title: Array vs Linked List

rows.label: Representation
values: Contiguous fixed-width slots; object payloads may be referenced.
Nodes contain payload and links; allocations can be dispersed.

rows.label: Indexed lookup
values: Θ(1) under a random-access word model.
Θ(n) from the head; traverse links to locate an index.

rows.label: Stable middle update
values: Θ(n) worst-case shifts; append is amortized O(1) with geometric growth.
O(1) relinking when node/predecessor is known; finding it can be Θ(n).

rows.label: Memory
values: Capacity slack; few backing allocations; copying during growth.
Per-node links, alignment and allocation overhead; no single uniform byte count.

rows.label: Locality and identity
values: Sequential slots favor scans. Reallocation or shifting can invalidate locations.
Stable node addresses until removal; pointer chasing can reduce locality.

rows.label: Typical use
values: Indexed sequences, DP storage, heaps, bulk processing.
Splicing known nodes and intrusive structures; not automatically faster for general inserts.

comparisons.guidance: Count location cost as well as update cost. Prefer a packed sequence for frequent scans/indexing; choose linked nodes when their identity and known-position relinking justify allocation and locality costs.

comparisons.title: Stack vs Queue

rows.label: Access rule
values: LIFO: newest unfinished state is removed first.
FIFO: oldest waiting item is removed first.

rows.label: Operations
values: push, pop and peek at one end.
enqueue at back, dequeue at front, peek at front.

rows.label: Cost with a suitable representation
values: O(1) linked operations or amortized O(1) array push.
O(1) linked operations or amortized O(1) circular-buffer operations; front array shifting is O(n).

rows.label: Memory
values: Tracks nested unfinished work; DFS may store a path/frontier.
Tracks arrival order or BFS frontier; width can dominate memory.

rows.label: Applications
values: Recursion, backtracking, expression parsing and undo.
BFS, buffering, scheduling and ordered work dispatch.

comparisons.guidance: Select the order required by the algorithm. Changing a BFS queue to a stack changes traversal behavior and removes the unweighted shortest-path discovery guarantee.

comparisons.title: BST vs Hash Table

rows.label: Invariant
values: All keys in the left subtree precede the node; right keys follow under the duplicate policy.
Hash-derived bucket/probe location plus a collision-resolution invariant.

rows.label: Lookup
values: O(h); O(log n) requires a balancing or distribution assumption.
Expected O(1) under suitable hashing/load assumptions; O(n) worst case.

rows.label: Order and ranges
values: Inorder traversal is sorted; predecessor, successor and bounded ranges are natural.
No general sorted-order guarantee; range queries generally require scanning or a second index.

rows.label: Key work
values: Each comparison may inspect multiple key bytes.
Hashing a long key itself costs time; equality still resolves collisions.

rows.label: Failure mode
values: An ordinary BST can degenerate into a chain.
Clustering, excessive load or adversarial collisions can destroy expected performance.

comparisons.guidance: Use hashing for equality lookup when its assumptions fit. Use balanced ordered trees for order-sensitive queries or logarithmic operation bounds. Neither bound treats arbitrarily long keys as free.

comparisons.title: AVL vs Red-Black Tree

rows.label: Balance invariant
values: Child heights differ by at most one at every node.
Color rules constrain black height and prevent adjacent red nodes.

rows.label: Height
values: O(log n), with a tighter height constraint.
O(log n), allowing more height variation.

rows.label: Repair
values: Maintain heights and rotate after violating balance; deletion may repair many ancestors.
Maintain colors and black height using recoloring/rotations; repair cases are different.

rows.label: Operations
values: Search, insert and delete have O(log n) worst-case time.
Search, insert and delete have O(log n) worst-case time.

rows.label: Engineering tradeoff
values: Tighter height can reduce lookup depth; metadata maintenance and update workload matter.
Looser balancing can suit mixed workloads; not a universal claim that every update is faster.

comparisons.guidance: Both provide ordered logarithmic operations. Compare the actual update/read workload and implementation, rather than declaring a winner from asymptotic bounds alone.

comparisons.title: BFS vs DFS

rows.label: Frontier
values: FIFO queue; explores by distance in edge count.
Recursion or LIFO stack; follows a branch before backtracking.

rows.label: Time
values: O(V+E) with adjacency lists and one discovery per vertex.
O(V+E) with adjacency lists and visited-state handling.

rows.label: Shortest paths
values: First discovery yields minimum edge count in unweighted graphs.
First discovered route need not be shortest.

rows.label: Memory
values: O(V) worst-case frontier/visited storage.
O(V) worst-case storage; recursion depth may reach V.

rows.label: Applications
values: Unweighted distances, multi-source propagation, levels.
Cycle structure, finishing times, topological order, low-link algorithms.

comparisons.guidance: Use BFS for minimum edge count. Use DFS when ancestor relationships and finishing order drive the proof. Representation and marking time matter to both complexity bounds.

comparisons.title: Dijkstra vs Bellman–Ford

rows.label: Weights
values: Requires nonnegative edge weights for the settled-distance proof.
Allows negative edges; detects reachable negative cycles.

rows.label: Strategy
values: Settle the smallest tentative distance using a priority queue.
Relax all edges repeatedly; paths with more edges propagate across rounds.

rows.label: Time
values: O((V+E) log V) with an appropriate heap implementation; duplicate-entry bounds also depend on E.
O(VE) worst case for the standard algorithm.

rows.label: Negative cycles
values: Outside the algorithm contract.
Distances to vertices reachable through a reachable negative cycle have no finite minimum.

rows.label: Memory
values: Distance/predecessor arrays and a heap; duplicate candidates may use O(E) space.
O(V) auxiliary arrays beyond graph storage.

comparisons.guidance: Check edge-weight assumptions before picking a faster algorithm. For a DAG, topological relaxation handles negative edges in O(V+E); for unweighted graphs BFS is simpler.

comparisons.title: Fenwick vs Segment Tree

rows.label: Stored summaries
values: Overlapping power-of-two prefix blocks selected by lowbit.
A hierarchy of interval aggregates.

rows.label: Query/update time
values: O(log n) prefix sum and point addition.
O(log n) range aggregation and point update for constant-time combines.

rows.label: Algebra
values: Standard range sum uses subtraction of prefixes; ordinary point updates use additive deltas.
Associative combine with identity supports a monoid; inverses are not generally required.

rows.label: Memory
values: O(n) entries, usually compact.
O(n) nodes/entries with larger representation constants in common layouts.

rows.label: Extensions
values: Range-update variants using transformed prefix formulas.
Lazy propagation requires a compatible update action; persistence and custom summaries need additional invariants.

comparisons.guidance: Choose Fenwick for simple additive prefix/range work and compact implementation. Choose a segment tree for richer associative summaries or composable range updates. Neither extension is valid without checking its algebra.

comparisons.title: Merge Sort vs Quick Sort

rows.label: Decomposition
values: Sort two halves, then merge sorted results.
Partition around a pivot, then sort the resulting regions.

rows.label: Time
values: Θ(n log n) for the usual top-down array implementation.
Expected Θ(n log n) with suitable randomization; Θ(n²) worst case without safeguards.

rows.label: Auxiliary memory
values: Typical array merging uses Θ(n) extra storage.
In-place partitioning plus call stack; naive recursion can reach Θ(n) depth.

rows.label: Stability
values: Stable when equal keys are taken from the left half first.
Typical in-place partitioning is not stable.

rows.label: Applications
values: Stable sorting, sequential merging and external-sort designs.
In-memory sorting with good locality; production hybrids add worst-case safeguards.

comparisons.guidance: Stability, allocation budget and worst-case guarantees are part of the selection. A textbook quicksort is not interchangeable with a production introspective sort.

comparisons.title: Prim vs Kruskal

rows.label: Selection
values: Prim grows a tree from a visited region using a cheapest crossing edge.
Kruskal processes all edges in nondecreasing weight and joins different components.

rows.label: State
values: Best crossing candidates and a visited set, often managed by a heap.
A disjoint-set structure tracking the current forest components.

rows.label: Time
values: O(E log V) with an adjacency-list heap approach, or O(V²) with a dense matrix.
O(E log E) sorting plus near-linear DSU operations.

rows.label: Disconnected input
values: Restart from unvisited vertices to obtain a minimum spanning forest.
Naturally produces a minimum spanning forest after processing all edges.

rows.label: Correctness
values: A light edge across the current cut is safe.
A light edge joining two forest components is safe; cycles are rejected.

comparisons.guidance: Both solve undirected spanning-tree/forest problems, not shortest paths. Compare graph density, input representation, and the cost of sorting versus maintaining a frontier.
